name: Methotrexate-associated lymphoproliferative disorders

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: No standardized formal criteria; diagnosis based on clinical, histopathological, and treatment response features

criteria.description: History of methotrexate therapy, typically for autoimmune disease
Histopathological evidence of lymphoproliferative disorder on biopsy
Partial or complete regression of lymphoproliferative lesions after methotrexate discontinuation
Evidence of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection in lesions (supportive but not mandatory)
Presence of lymphadenopathy, extranodal masses, or systemic symptoms

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of lymphoproliferative histology in a patient with methotrexate exposure and regression of lesions after methotrexate withdrawal
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other lymphomas and consideration of clinical context

pathognomonic.notes: Enlarged lymph nodes often in cervical or mediastinal regions
Commonly involves skin, lungs, or gastrointestinal tract

pathognomonic.symptomName: Spontaneous regression of lymphoproliferative lesions after methotrexate withdrawal
pathognomonic.notes: Characteristic feature distinguishing MTX-LPD from other lymphomas
searchTerms: lymph node swelling improves after stopping methotrexate
spontaneous shrinkage of lymph lesions post drug withdrawal
regression of lymphoproliferation after methotrexate stop

common.symptomName: B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)

common.notes: Enlargement of liver and spleen due to lymphoid infiltration
Secondary to bone marrow involvement or chronic disease
searchTerms: fatigue related to low red blood cells
red spots or bumps on skin

occasional.notes: Rarely reported due to nerve infiltration or paraneoplastic effects

rare.notes: Due to immunosuppression from disease or treatment
searchTerms: severe infections due to weak immunity

laboratory: Presence of EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in biopsy specimens
imaging: CT or PET-CT showing lymphadenopathy and extranodal masses
Resolution of lesions on imaging after methotrexate withdrawal
genetic: No specific genetic mutations; clonality demonstrated by immunoglobulin or T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies
other: Histopathology showing polymorphic or monomorphic lymphoid proliferation
Immunohistochemistry positive for B-cell or T-cell markers depending on subtype

distinguishingFeatures: Lack of regression after methotrexate withdrawal
Similar EBV association but different clinical context

redFlags: Rapidly enlarging lymphadenopathy or extranodal masses
Failure of lesion regression after methotrexate discontinuation
Development of severe systemic symptoms or organ dysfunction
references: Swerdlow SH, et al. WHO Classification of Tumours of Haematopoietic and Lymphoid Tissues, Revised 4th Edition. IARC; 2017.
Tokuhira M, et al. Methotrexate-associated lymphoproliferative disorders: Clinicopathological features and prognosis. Pathol Int. 2019.
Kameda T, et al. Clinical features and outcomes of methotrexate-associated lymphoproliferative disorders. Mod Rheumatol. 2017.
